content: 1. Practical Procedures for Pediatric Care: Before performing any procedure on a child, explain the process to the parents or the child (if they are old enough to understand). Discuss any potential risks and obtain informed consent. Ensure the environment is warm to prevent hypothermia, especially for young infants. Adequate lighting is essential for visibility. Older children should be informed about what will happen during the procedure. Administer analgesia if necessary to manage pain. 2. Administering Injections: Always check if the child has had any adverse reactions to medications in the past. Wash your hands thoroughly and use disposable needles and syringes. Clean the injection site with an antiseptic solution. Verify the correct drug dosage and draw the appropriate amount into the syringe. Expel any air from the syringe before injecting. Record the name and dosage of the drug administered. Intramuscular Injections: For children over 2 years old, inject into the outer thigh or the upper, outer quadrant of the buttock, avoiding the sciatic nerve. For younger or severely malnourished children, use the outer side of the thigh midway between the hip and knee or the deltoid muscle in the upper arm. Insert the needle (23–25 gauge) at a 90° angle (or 45° in the thigh). Pull back the plunger to check for blood; if blood is present, reposition the needle slightly and try again. Administer the drug slowly and remove the needle. Apply firm pressure with a cotton swab over the injection site. Subcutaneous Injections: Select the site as described for intramuscular injections. Insert the needle (23–25 gauge) at a 45° angle into the subcutaneous fatty tissue, avoiding the underlying muscle. Pull back the plunger to check for blood; if blood is present, reposition the needle slightly and try again. Administer the drug slowly and remove the needle. Apply firm pressure with cotton wool over the injection site. 3. Intravenous (IV) Cannulation: Choose a suitable vein for cannulation, such as the cephalic vein in the antecubital fossa or the fourth interdigital vein on the dorsum of the hand in children over 2 months old. Clean the skin with an antiseptic solution. Insert the cannula or butterfly needle into the vein and secure it with tape. Flush the cannula with normal saline after insertion and after each injection to maintain patency. Monitor for complications such as superficial skin infections, thrombophlebitis, or fever. If infection occurs, remove the cannula, apply a warm compress, and consider antibiotic treatment if fever persists. 4. Intraosseous Infusion: This method is used in emergencies when venous access is not possible. The preferred site is the proximal tibia, specifically the anteromedial surface at the junction of the upper and middle third, avoiding the epiphyseal plate. Clean the skin with an antiseptic solution. Insert the needle at a 90° angle using a gentle twisting motion. Stop advancing the needle when resistance decreases or when bone marrow is aspirated. Confirm placement by aspirating 1 mL of marrow contents. Flush with normal saline and monitor for infiltration or leakage. Start the infusion if no complications are observed. Remove the needle as soon as venous access is established, and do not continue intraosseous infusion for more than 8 hours. 5. Central Venous Cannulation: This should only be performed when IV access is urgently required. Common sites include the external jugular vein or the femoral vein. For the external jugular vein, position the child with the head turned to one side and slightly lower than the body. Clean the skin with an antiseptic solution and identify the vein. Insert the needle in the direction of the clavicle and proceed with cannulation. For the femoral vein, position the child supine with the hip slightly extended and the knee flexed. Clean the skin, palpate the femoral artery, and locate the femoral vein, which lies medial to the artery. Insert the needle at a 10° angle to the skin and secure the cannula with sutures and sterile dressings. 6. Venous Cut-Down: This method is used when other forms of venous access are not feasible. Identify the long saphenous vein near the medial malleolus. Infiltrate the skin with 1% lignocaine and make a perpendicular incision over the vein. Bluntly dissect the subcutaneous tissue, isolate a segment of the vein, and tie off the distal end. Insert the cannula into the vein and secure it with ligatures. Attach a syringe filled with normal saline to confirm patency. 7. Monitoring and Complications: Regularly monitor the infusion site for signs of infection, infiltration, or other complications. Keep the site clean and dry, and ensure the cannula is securely fixed. For intraosseous or central venous access, monitor the clinical response and fluid flow. Remove the cannula or needle as soon as alternative access is available.
